stories.title: Retail Landlords Need to Underwrite Their Tenants’ Customer Base, Too
stories.excerpt: Landlords underwrite the retail tenant. But they almost never underwrite the tenant’s customer. They should. That gap costs landlords money, and it is fixable before a listing goes live. The standard leasing process is too reactive: Review comparable rents, post the space on Crexi and LoopNet, wait for responses, and then vet an operator’s finances. Mark Kvetkovskiy. None of that tells you whether enough of that retailer’s customers live near the space. If they do not, the risk rises of tenant failure, months of vacancy, and another round of commissions and negotiations. The better approach is to flip the process. Instead of waiting to see who shows up, start by studying who lives near the space. How do nearby households spend? Which categories over-index locally? Does the neighborhood support an everyday concept, a destination brand, or something in between? Answer those questions first, and you can define the customer already walking the neighborhood’s streets. Then, identify the brands that serve that customer and approach them directly about the vacancy. Proactive outreach can reduce days on market and the vacancy costs that come with them. Consider a hypothetical vacant restaurant at Rivington and Ludlow streets on Manhattan’s Lower East Side. I analyzed the 2026 Esri Consumer Spending Survey and Esri Market Potential data for the area within a five-minute walk. Esri’s modeled data draws on consumer surveys, demographic segmentation and household spending patterns. It is directional, not a record of observed transactions. Esri estimates that households in that walking area spend $50,243,250 annually on food and beverages away from home, or about $5,043 per household. The market-potential data then sharpens the picture. Some 20.4 percent of adults in the area visited a fine-dining restaurant in the previous six months, an index of 124, or 24 percent above the U.S. average. Among fine-dining consumers, 29.01 percent spend more than $
bullets: Retail landlords underwrite tenant finances but rarely analyze customer demographics.
Proactive neighborhood customer profiling reduces vacancy and leasing costs.
Gap between tenant underwriting and customer demand creates avoidable tenant failures.
stories.summary: Retail landlords follow reactive leasing: post space, wait for offers, then vet tenants. The better approach flips the process—study neighborhood demographics and spending patterns first, then recruit brands that serve that customer base directly. This proactive strategy reduces days on market, vacancy costs, and commissions, because it ensures tenant-customer alignment before lease signing.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily development. However, retail health affects mixed-use and ground-floor demand in multifamily projects; developers should apply similar customer-demand analysis to retail components of residential buildings to ensure anchor tenancy strength and resident amenity quality.

stories.title: Inflation Is Down. But Consumers Aren’t Out of the Woods Yet
stories.excerpt: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 3.4% year over year in July. Meanwhile, the core CPI, which excludes food and energy costs, rose 2.5%. Both measures fell slightly month over month. They also matched market expectations and suggested that inflationary pressures could be moderating. A recent Marcus & Millichap report supported that possibility, noting that despite continued turmoil in the Middle East and its potential impact on supply chains, the latest readings could “modestly ease immediate pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.” Rent Growth Continues Muted Housing remains one of the largest contributors to the core CPI, with the Owners’ Equivalent Rent (OER) accounting for much of the metric. Also counted are apartment rents. These increased by 1.3%, compared with the 2.1% increase the year before. At the same time, real average hourly earnings declined 0.1%. This suggests that consumers’ purchasing power remains under pressure even as inflation moderates. Consumer Spending Faces Headwinds Food prices continued to climb in July, with year-over-year grocery and restaurant prices increasing by 2.7% and 3.4%, respectively. “Although this divergence may suggest consumers remain willing to spend on discretionary dining, it may also signal vulnerability if household purchasing power weakens further,” Marcus & Millichap said. Retail property fundamentals were mixed. Vacancy remains 60 basis points below its historical average, as space demand remains volatile. Net space relinquishment occurred in three of the past six quarters. The report suggested that retailers are working in a resilient consumer environment but are selective about spending. Hospitality Could Feel the Pressure Leisure spending is under pressure, too. The Leisure and Hospitality sector lost 40,000 jobs nationally in July, while hotel occupancy declined 20 basis points in June despite World Cup travel demand. “With transportation costs still elevated and travel dem
bullets: CPI at 3.4% year-over-year in July; core CPI 2.5%—both moderating.
Apartment rents rose 1.3% year-over-year (vs. 2.1% prior year); real wage growth declined 0.1%.
Housing remains largest core CPI contributor; consumer purchasing power under pressure despite inflation moderation.
stories.summary: July inflation data shows headline CPI at 3.4% and core at 2.5%, both slightly easing monthly. Apartment rents decelerated to 1.3% year-over-year growth versus 2.1% the prior year. Real average hourly earnings declined 0.1%, signaling squeezed household purchasing power even as inflation moderates. Consumers may remain cautious on discretionary spending.
stories.impact: Rent growth deceleration signals softening demand tailwinds in multifamily; combined with declining real wages, renter affordability pressures persist, potentially limiting ability to push rents in secondary/tertiary markets. Developers should stress-test underwriting for flatter rent escalators and reconsider value-add repositioning assumptions.

stories.title: Retail Regains Its Footing as Demand Returns and Supply Stays Soft
stories.excerpt: After a soft first quarter, the retail sector regained positive momentum in Q2 as tenant demand returned, vacancies remained stable and new construction stayed limited. According to second-quarter reports from CBRE, Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, JLL and Lee & Associates, the combination is creating a favorable setup for landlords and investors, even as retailers contend with increasingly selective consumers. Absorption Retail demand returned in the second quarter, reversing the Q1 negative absorption created, in part, by multiple move-outs. Ongoing tenant demand and the backfilling of vacant space in Q2 helped overcome that first-quarter softness. Some retail categories also benefited from back-to-school spending, with clothing, sporting goods and school supplies among the areas reporting sales growth. Construction New retail supply remained limited, with higher construction costs and continued financing challenges discouraging speculative development. Most new projects are concentrated in build-to-suit and grocery-anchored developments, where tenant demand provides greater certainty. Sunbelt markets continue to account for the lion’s share of construction activity. The supply constraints are helping support modest rent growth nationwide. Investment Investors remain actively interested in retail, with first-half 2026 sales volume reaching $33 billion, a 14% increase from the same period last year. Stronger sales momentum is putting pressure on pricing and contributing to cap-rate compression. Outlook Retail construction is expected to remain sluggish and concentrated in select Sunbelt metros, keeping vacancies low into 2027. Consumers are likely to remain value-conscious, benefiting discount retailers as well as specialty and off-price centers. Well-capitalized retailers and those with strong value propositions should remain better positioned to handle potential headwinds. Limited new supply should continue to support rent growth, while landlords and tenant
bullets: Retail vacancy stable in Q2; tenant demand returned after soft Q1.
New construction remains limited; favorable landlord/investor setup emerging.
Retailers contend with increasingly selective consumers despite sector momentum.
stories.summary: According to Q2 reports from CBRE, Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, JLL, and Lee & Associates, the retail sector regained momentum after a weak first quarter. Tenant demand rebounded, vacancy stayed flat, and new construction stayed restrained—a combination favoring landlords and investors. Retailers, however, face more discriminating consumers.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily. Healthy retail—particularly limited new supply—may support co-tenancy value and foot traffic for mixed-use multifamily developments, but core residential demand drivers (jobs, in-migration) remain the primary lever.

stories.title: How the “Vanity Economy” Is Impacting Retail
stories.excerpt: Social media and its influencers have turned appearance into a powerful consumer category, and shopping centers offering such services are the beneficiaries, according to a recent CBRE report. Influencer marketing, celebrity beauty partnerships and growing interest in health and wellness have fueled what CBRE calls the “vanity economy,” which encompasses beauty services, cosmetics and specialty fitness retailers. Consumers spent about $132 billion on appearance-enhancing products in 2025, up from $86 billion in 2020. Those categories also accounted for 37.5% of total leased space as of Q2 2026, according to CoStar data cited by CBRE. Where the Numbers Are The global beauty market is now valued at approximately $450 billion, according to McKinsey data included the CBRE report. That market is expected to grow at an annual rate of about 5% through 2030. Cosmetics are one major contributor, as consumer spending on these products increased 38% over the past five years to $25.4 billion. Furthermore, brick-and-mortar stores remain the primary channel for consumers to buy their beauty products, accounting for 74% of sales. Physical stores also give consumers a place to discover new products and replenish products they already use. Services are another vanity economy component, consisting of beauty and nail salons and barbershops, is expected to grow by 10% annually, according to Kentley Insights, as introduced in the CBRE report. Additionally, consumers spent $45.7 billion on fitness centers in 2025. CBRE said these centers can generate regular visits that benefit other shopping-center tenants. What It Means for Retail For shopping-center owners and operators, beauty and wellness tenants can help generate traffic and increase dwell time, creating what CBRE describes as a complementary retail ecosystem. Beauty services and boutique fitness can also be concentrated in markets with favorable demographics. That makes these operators more than just another tenant category: Their
bullets: Vanity economy (beauty, cosmetics, wellness) reached $132B in 2025, up from $86B in 2020.
Beauty and fitness now account for 37.5% of leased retail space (Q2 2026); global beauty market valued at $450B.
Brick-and-mortar stores drive 74% of beauty product sales; expected 5% annual growth through 2030.
stories.summary: Social media and influencer marketing have fueled a 'vanity economy' in retail. Consumers spent $132 billion on appearance-enhancing products in 2025 (up 53% from 2020), with cosmetics spending up 38% over five years to $25.4 billion. Beauty, cosmetics, and specialty fitness account for 37.5% of all leased retail space. Physical retail remains the dominant sales channel (74%), and the global beauty market is forecast to grow 5% annually through 2030.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily development alone. However, the strength and durability of beauty/wellness retail creates a tenant stabilizer and drives foot traffic in mixed-use urban multifamily projects, especially in walkable neighborhoods with affluent renters (NYC, LA, Miami submarkets). Developers should actively court beauty/wellness anchors and retailers for ground-floor retail components.

stories.title: T&E Development Buys West Chelsea Site for $34M From PPHE Hotel Group
stories.excerpt: A development site in Manhattan’s West Chelsea area previously conceived for hotel and luxury residences in 2019 by an international hospitality firm is now poised for a new residential journey. Amsterdam-based PPHE Hotel Group sold the property at 538-542 West 29th Street to Brooklyn-based T&E Development for $33.5 million in a deal that closed late Thursday afternoon, Commercial Observer has learned. Colliers represented the seller with a team led by Zach Redding, Dylan Kane and Jared King. Sporn Group’s Lenny Sporn arranged the sale on behalf of the buyer. Crain’s New York Business first reported that the deal was set to close this summer. PPHE Hotel Group announced in March 2019 it had formed a joint venture with developer Largo to acquire the vacant lot for around $42 million, with plans to build a 98-key hotel and 55 condos. An entity connected to PPHE field demolition permits for the project in late 2023, Crain’s reported at the time. Greg Hegarty, co-CEO of PPHE, said in a February statement on the pending sale that “significant changes to the regulatory landscape” for ground-up development of hotel projects in New York following its 2019 acquisition contributed to the decision to part ways with the property. The 9,875-square-foot vacant lot between 10th and 11th avenues has 74,063 square feet of development potential under New York City’s C6-3 zoning within the Special West Chelsea District and will not require an affordable housing component, according to Colliers. T&E recently completed a 54-unit condo development called the Florian at 350 East 18th Street in Manhattan’s Gramercy Park. Redding said the property is one of the few remaining unconstrained development sites in West Chelsea and would be well positioned as a residential project given there is only one condo building currently under construction between West 20th and West 30th streets. He noted that nearby condo developments have netted average sales of roughly $2,884 per square fo
bullets: T&E Development acquired West Chelsea site (Manhattan) from PPHE Hotel Group for $33.5M.
Property at 538–542 West 29th Street was originally conceived as 98-key hotel + 55 condos in 2019.
Shift from hotel/condo to pure residential signals changed market demand and capital allocation in Chelsea.
stories.summary: T&E Development bought a 538–542 West 29th Street development site in Manhattan's West Chelsea from PPHE Hotel Group for $33.5 million, closing late July. PPHE had initially acquired the vacant lot in 2019 with Largo for ~$42 million, planning a 98-key hotel and 55 condos. After filing demolition permits in late 2023, PPHE pivoted to a sale, signaling a strategic shift away from hotel development.
stories.impact: Signals retreat from hotel development in West Chelsea and renewed focus on residential-only strategies, likely due to softer hotel market dynamics and stronger multifamily capital flows. Developer should monitor whether T&E builds pure multifamily or mixed-use; if pure multifamily, it confirms West Chelsea rental demand strength and potential upside for comparable projects in Chelsea, Meatpacking District, and Hudson Yards subareas.

stories.title: Cyber Risk Management Firm Signs Five-Year Renewal of Midtown Offices
stories.excerpt: JLL represented SecurityScorecard, a global leader in cyber risk intelligence, in a five-year renewal of its full-floor headquarters at 1140 Ave. of the Americas in Midtown Manhattan. A tenant since 2023, the company occupies 8,475 square feet across a full floor featuring a large private outdoor terrace and collaborative workspace. The Cushman & Wakefield team of Josh Kuriloff, Matthias Li, Heather Thomas, Pierce Hance and Nicole Estevez represented the landlord in leasing negotiations. JLL managing director Valentin Stobetsky represented SecurityScorecard. “1140 Ave. of the Americas offers everything a fast-growing technology company like SecurityScorecard is looking for,” said Stobetsky. “It has a premier Midtown location, outstanding transit access, modern amenities and a unique full-floor office with an expansive private outdoor terrace that enhances the employee experience. It’s an ideal environment for attracting top talent and supporting the company’s next phase of growth.” The post Cyber Risk Management Firm Signs Five-Year Renewal of Midtown Offices appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: SecurityScorecard (cyber risk firm) renewed five-year lease at 1140 Ave. of Americas, Midtown Manhattan.
Tenant occupies full floor, 8,475 sq. ft., with private outdoor terrace; tenant since 2023.
Tech company renewal signals office occupancy stability in Midtown among fast-growing tech firms.
stories.summary: SecurityScorecard, a cyber risk intelligence firm, renewed its full-floor headquarters at 1140 Avenue of the Americas in Midtown Manhattan for five years. The company occupies 8,475 square feet and has been a tenant since 2023. The landlord (represented by Cushman & Wakefield) and the tenant (represented by JLL) emphasized the location's premium transit access, amenities, and outdoor space as key to talent retention.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily. Tech company office renewals in Midtown indicate sustained corporate presence and job stability in Manhattan's tech corridor, which supports baseline rental demand for multifamily in outer boroughs (Long Island City, Astoria) and Downtown Brooklyn where tech workers increasingly locate for affordability and commute.

stories.title: Data Centers Push Into Frontier Markets
stories.excerpt: One trend emerging from JLL’s Midyear North America Data Center Report is that developers continue to hit the power wall. This obstacle is stretching timelines in established hubs, encouraging developers to examine space in areas that were once outside of the industry’s main hubs. Working the Energy Crisis Sean Farney The power challenge raises the question of where developers can find the needed electricity to get new centers off the ground. JLL Vice President of Data Center Strategy Sean Farney told Connect CRE that developers are experimenting with alternative power solutions to bypass grid constraints and improve development timelines. Utilities are directing developers toward co-located generation and on-site battery storage, while microgrids are also a potential solution for addressing grid constraints. Those microgrids, however, remain under regulatory scrutiny. Direct partnerships with utilities are also becoming more common. Despite these efforts, long interconnection timelines remain a problem. Farney said new Commonwealth Edison projects in Chicago have four- to five-year delivery timelines, along with letter-of-credit commitments of approximately $46,000 per megawatt annually for 10 years. “Grid limitations in Columbus, OH, are pushing users to secondary markets with available capacity,” he added. Mining the Frontier The reports refer to these secondary regions as “frontier markets,” noting that 77% of capacity under construction is located in such areas. These markets offer several advantages in addition to greater power availability. They provide builder-friendly regulatory environments, enough land to accommodate large campuses, lower operating costs and room for long-term expansion. Farney said grid constraints in Columbus are pushing overflow development toward the Ohio cities of Van Wert, Lima and Canton. At the same time, Southern Virginia and the I-95 corridor are attracting data center projects from nearby Loudoun and Prince William counties. “W
bullets: Data center developers hitting 'power wall'; grid constraints pushing projects to secondary markets.
Chicago Commonwealth Edison new projects face 4–5 year interconnection timelines; Columbus, OH utilities directing users to secondaries.
Alternative solutions (co-gen, battery storage, microgrids) and direct utility partnerships emerging; microgrids face regulatory scrutiny.
stories.summary: According to JLL's Midyear North America Data Center Report, data center developers are constrained by limited grid capacity in established hubs (Chicago, Columbus), pushing them toward frontier and secondary markets. Chicago Commonwealth Edison projects face 4–5 year delivery timelines with $46,000/MW/year letter-of-credit commitments. Developers are exploring co-generation, on-site battery storage, and microgrids to bypass grid constraints, though regulatory hurdles remain.
stories.impact: Data center migration to secondary markets may signal infrastructure investment and job growth in those regions (e.g., Columbus, Indianapolis, Raleigh), indirectly strengthening demand for workforce housing. Multifamily developers in secondary markets should monitor data center project pipelines and partner with utility/infrastructure announcements to identify emerging employment hubs and early-stage demand windows before land appreciates significantly.

stories.title: L.A. County Investment Sales Jump 28% in July Thanks to Multifamily
stories.excerpt: Commercial real estate investment sales accelerated across Los Angeles County in July, with multifamily accounting for the majority of capital deployed. About 7.25 million square feet of commercial property traded for $2.1 billion last month, NAI Capital reported Thursday, citing CoStar data. Compared to July 2025, almost 22 percent more square footage traded hands during July to make for a 28.5 percent jump in dollar volume. Compared with July 2024, sales volume climbed 75 percent. The gains came despite elevated borrowing costs, with long-term Treasury yields remaining near multiyear highs. Multifamily dominated, with 3.43 million square feet changing hands for $1.22 billion — accounting for 58 percent of all investment during the month in L.A. County. Sales volume increased 55 percent since last year, and almost 166 percent compared to July 2024. Average pricing rose 28.7 percent to $376 per square foot. People look at the Los Angeles skyline from Griffith Observatory. PHOTO: Matt McNulty - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images Retail also posted broad gains. About 1.23 million square feet sold for $402 million, pushing dollar volume up 40 percent from a year ago, and nearly doubling the July 2024 total. Retail square footage traded has climbed 135 percent over the same two-year period. Industrial faces a more complicated environment. About 1.33 million square feet traded in July, which is almost 71 percent higher since 2025, but dollar volume remained about flat at $214 million, and average pricing fell 3.6 percent to $273 per square foot. Office was the only major property type to decline in both sales volume and square footage. About 1.26 million square feet sold for $262 million, down 9.7 percent and 23.4 percent, respectively, from July 2025. Average pricing dropped 23.5 percent to $250 per square foot. bullets: L.A. County CRE investment sales jumped 28.5% to $2.1B in July; 75% gain vs. July 2024.
Multifamily dominated with 3.43M sq. ft. for $1.22B (58% of all capital); sales up 55% YoY and 166% vs. July 2024.
Multifamily average pricing rose 28.7% to $376/sq. ft.; gains despite elevated borrowing costs.
stories.summary: Commercial real estate investment sales in Los Angeles County surged 28.5% in July to $2.1 billion, with multifamily accounting for 58% of capital deployed. Multifamily sales volume jumped 55% year-over-year and 166% versus July 2024, with average pricing climbing 28.7% to $376 per square foot. This acceleration occurred despite elevated Treasury yields and high borrowing costs.
stories.impact: Strong L.A. County multifamily capital flows and pricing momentum signal sustained investor appetite and rent fundamentals in LA metros (West LA, Santa Monica, Downtown, Mid-City). Developers should accelerate land acquisition and entitlement timelines in LA primary markets before pricing accelerates further; secondary LA submarkets (San Fernando Valley, Long Beach, Inland Empire) may offer better entry points with similar demand tailwinds.

stories.title: New York City’s Technology Labor Market Has Surpassed San Francisco: Report
stories.excerpt: It’s official. New York is employing more tech workers than the San Francisco Bay area. According to an annual CBRE report on North American tech talent, the New York metropolitan area’s tech workforce reached 394,300 in 2025. The stat marks an 8.4 percent increase from 2022 that added 30,640 jobs. Meanwhile, San Francisco’s tech employment fell by 6 percent over the same period, totaling 375,730 jobs in 2025. This is the first time in the report’s 13-year history that the Big Apple has come out ahead. The city’s diversified job market helped set it apart, Colin Yasukochi, executive director of CBRE’s tech insights center, told Commercial Observer. “What really pushed New York past the San Francisco Bay Area has been the job reductions that we’ve seen [in San Francisco], with a lot of the announced layoffs, and the fact that New York has continued to grow,” Yasukochi said. San Francisco remains in North America’s top spot for its pool of tech talent, however, ranked across 13 metrics. The report, which analyzed the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and LinkedIn data, found that tech jobs make up more than 10 percent of total employment in San Francisco, compared to just 4.2 percent in New York. But a whopping 61 percent of San Francisco’s tech talent works directly in the tech industry, according to CBRE’s report, leaving its general labor market vulnerable. In New York City, just 34 percent of its tech workers work within the industry, while 21 percent work in tech roles in finance, insurance and real estate industries (otherwise known as FIRE). “[That] has given New York resilience from the tech downturn that broadly started in 2022, in terms of employment,” Yasukochi said. “But, obviously, with the artificial intelligence industry coming into play, that’s turned around quite substantially in the last year.” Yasukochi added that New York also benefits from a massive university infrastructure and lower wages than San Francisco, on average, for
bullets: NYC metro tech workforce reached 394,300 in 2025; +8.4% since 2022 (+30,640 jobs).
San Francisco Bay Area tech employment fell 6% over same period to 375,730 in 2025—first time NYC ahead in 13-year report.
NYC's diversified job market offset SF's announced layoffs; SF still ranks #1 on talent pool quality across 13 metrics.
stories.summary: New York City's tech workforce (394,300 jobs in 2025) has surpassed San Francisco's (375,730 jobs) for the first time in a 13-year CBRE report. NYC added 30,640 tech jobs since 2022 (+8.4%), while SF declined 6% over the same period due to announced layoffs. NYC's diversified job market drove the milestone, though SF remains ranked first overall on talent metrics.
stories.impact: NYC's tech employment lead signals sustained in-migration of young, high-earning workers to the metro, strengthening rental demand in tech-heavy submarkets (Long Island City, Astoria, Downtown Brooklyn, Williamsburg) and Manhattan (Flatiron, Murray Hill, LES). Developers should prioritize apartments near transit/tech clusters and target millennial/Gen-Z renters; expect continued rent growth and lower vacancy in NYC tech-corridor neighborhoods through 2025–2026.

stories.title: Principal Financial Group Loans $32M to Refi Queens Shopping Center
stories.excerpt: An affiliate of Mattone Investors secured $32 million to refinance Springnex Plaza, a 96,028-square-foot shopping center anchored by a Stop & Shop supermarket in the Queens neighborhood of Springfield Gardens. Principal Financial Group provided the debt, while Northmarq’s Robert Delitsky and Charles Cotsalas arranged the transaction. Delitsky noted in a statement that Mattone Investors first developed Springnex Plaza six years ago and “have done a fabulous job maintaining very strong occupancy” since then. “Supermarket-anchored shopping centers like Springnex Plaza will continue to attract very strong lender interest in today’s market,” Cotsalas added in the same statement. Located at 134-40 Springfield Boulevard, Springnex Plaza sits on 5.58 acres of land and is 100 percent occupied. Besides Stop & Shop, tenants include an IHOP, fashion retailer Ashley Stewart and Northwell Health GoHealth Urgent Care. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Principal Financial Group loaned $32M to refinance Springnex Plaza, 96,028 sq. ft. shopping center, Queens.
Stop & Shop–anchored, 100% occupied, 5.58 acres in Springfield Gardens; developed by Mattone Investors six years ago.
Lender interest in supermarket-anchored centers remains strong despite elevated rates; debt availability supportive.
stories.summary: Mattone Investors secured a $32 million refinance from Principal Financial Group for Springnex Plaza, a 96,028-square-foot supermarket-anchored shopping center in Springfield Gardens, Queens. The center is 100% leased, features a Stop & Shop anchor plus IHOP, Ashley Stewart, and Northwell Health GoHealth Urgent Care, and sits on 5.58 acres. Northmarq arranged the transaction, noting strong lender appetite for well-maintained supermarket-anchored assets.
stories.impact: Strong debt availability for supermarket-anchored retail in outer-borough Queens signals lender confidence in recession-resistant, essential-service-anchored properties. Developers planning mixed-use or multifamily-retail projects in Queens/outer boroughs should prioritize grocery anchors to secure favorable financing terms and lower cap rates; supermarket co-tenancy also drives foot traffic and supports residential rents in ground-floor retail communities.
